busa1980watson.title: The Annals of Humanities Computing: The Index Thomisticus (Computers and the Humanities 14(2), pp. 83-90) — the 1949 IBM meeting
busa1980watson.author: Roberto Busa SJ
busa1980watson.quote: I knew, the day I was to meet Thomas J. Watson, Sr., that he had on his desk a report which said that IBM machines could never do what I wanted. I had seen in the waiting room a small poster imprinted with the words: "The difficult we do right away; the impossible takes a little longer," (IBM always loved slogans). I took it with me into Mr. Watson's office. ... He agreed that IBM would cooperate with my project until it was completed "provided that you do not change IBM into International Busa Machines." I had already informed him that, because my superiors had given me time, encouragement, their blessings and much holy water, but unfortunately no money, I could recompense IBM in any way except financially.
supports: the report on Watson's desk saying IBM machines could never do it
the waiting-room slogan Busa carried into the office
Busa could pay IBM nothing financially
Watson appointed Paul Tasman to assist

busa1980method.title: The Annals of Humanities Computing: The Index Thomisticus (Computers and the Humanities 14(2), pp. 83-90) — cards, sorting and lemmatising
busa1980method.author: Roberto Busa SJ
busa1980method.quote: It was clear to me, however, that to process texts containing more than ten million words, I had to look for some type of machinery. ... The first was to establish a file of punched cards, with one word on each card including reference and typological codes. ... Therefore, a team of ten priests worked with me for two full years to design a Latin machine dictionary. Called the Lexicon Electronicum Latinum (LEL), it is a set of tables by which a computer is able to lemmatize the words of Latin texts. I defined lemmatizing as two operations: (1) grouping all the forms of an inflected word (e.g., sum, es ... fui, fuisti ... essem, esses, fore, futurus ...) under their 'lemma,' i.e., the title or entry-word which represents it in a dictionary (here, the verb sum), and (2) coding the morphological categories of each form and lemma. For this, we first punched, sequenced and numbered the 90 000 lemmas in the Forcellini's Lexicon Totius Latinitatis (Padua, 1940). Then, we alphabetically sorted all the words of our texts and got a list of 130 000 graphically different forms of words occurring there.
supports: more than ten million words in the corpus
one word on each card, with its reference
alphabetical sort of every word of the texts
ten priests, two full years, to build the lemmatising tables
lemmatising defined as grouping inflected forms under a lemma

busa1980cost.title: The Annals of Humanities Computing: The Index Thomisticus (Computers and the Humanities 14(2), pp. 83-90) — the cost of the thirty years
busa1980cost.author: Roberto Busa SJ
busa1980cost.quote: The ratio of human work to machine time was more than 100 : 1. Computer hours were less than 10 000 while man hours were much more than one million. In fact we had to scan our texts word by word with human eyes and fingers at least 9 times: twice for pre-editing; once for punching; once for verifying; twice (two people each) for checking; twice for lemmatizing and sorting the homographs; and once for final arrangements and checkings. ... I was able to complete my IT 33 years after the conception of the project and 30 years after my first meeting with IBM.
supports: fewer than 10 000 computer hours against more than a million man hours
human-to-machine work ratio of more than 100 : 1
the texts scanned by eye at least nine times
completed 30 years after the first IBM meeting

busa1980first.title: The Annals of Humanities Computing: The Index Thomisticus (Computers and the Humanities 14(2), pp. 83-90) — the 1951 sample volume and the hand-built precursor
busa1980first.author: Roberto Busa SJ
busa1980first.quote: My next step was to write out by hand 10 000 3" X 5" cards, each containing a sentence with the word in or a word connected with in. Grand games of solitaire followed. ... In 1951 at the XVIII World Conference of Documentation held in Rome, my volume entitled S. Thomae Aquinatis Hymnorum Ritualium: Varia Specimina Concordantiarum: A First Example of a Word Index Automatically Compiled and Printed by IBM Punched Card Machines (Milano: Bocca 1951) was exhibited.
supports: 10 000 hand-written cards for the doctoral thesis on in
the 1951 Varia Specimina Concordantiarum, exhibited in Rome, as the first published output

unverified: The printed Index Thomisticus as 56 folio volumes published 1974-1980 by Frommann-Holzboog, and the 1992 CD-ROM. Both appear in Wikipedia's Index Thomisticus article, which was opened, but no primary or publisher source for either was reachable; neither figure appears in the prose or on a card.

The exact corpus size of 10,631,980 words. Busa's own 1980 article says 'more than ten million words' in one place and '10 600 000 words' in another; the precise figure comes only from secondary sources. The prose uses Busa's own wording.

November 1949 as the month of the Watson meeting, and IBM's headquarters address at 590 Madison Avenue. Both appear in search summaries of Steven E. Jones's 2016 book, which was not opened; Busa's own article dates the visit only to 1949.

That the IBM sorter could order cards on one field per pass, so each analysis decision cost another pass over the whole deck. Plausible for period unit-record equipment, but Tasman's 1957 'Literary Data Processing' (IBM Journal of Research and Development 1(3), 249-256) could not be opened and Busa 1980 does not state it.
Busa's age when the printed index was finished.

Who wrote the report on Watson's desk. Busa 1980 says only that IBM assigned 'someone' to examine the project and that Watson 'had on his desk a report which said that IBM machines could never do what I wanted'; it never attributes the report to IBM engineers. The cards now say only what the article says.
